by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is a firearm, motor vehicle, apparel item, or item of jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Classify by the statutory category: firearms under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(10), each motor vehicle as a candidate under § 33-1125(8), wearing apparel under § 33-1125(1), and only engagement or wedding rings under § 33-1125(4). In EC, a value or aggregate ceiling limits protection rather than citation eligibility, and the one-vehicle language does not require final portfolio allocation among separately listed vehicle candidates.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an otherwise matching firearm or vehicle solely for exceeding its ceiling. Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, or other non-apparel adornment as wearing apparel, and do not extend the ring exemption to jewelry that is not an engagement or wedding ring.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is a firearm, motor vehicle, apparel item, or item of jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Classify before valuing: use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(10) for firearms up to $2,000, § 33-1125(8) for each separately listed motor-vehicle candidate up to $15,000, § 33-1125(1) for actual wearing apparel up to $500, and § 33-1125(4) only for engagement or wedding rings up to $2,000. For each eligible alternative, report the lesser of the whole asset's value and its stated ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, watch, or other adornment as wearing apparel, extend the ring exemption to jewelry that is not an engagement or wedding ring, or perform a final allocation between separately listed vehicle candidates.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is a residence, homestead-sale proceeds, or property owned by married debtors.
by_task.procedure: For a qualifying occupied homestead, use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1101(A); for qualifying identifiable sale proceeds, separately test § 33-1101(C). Treat § 33-1101(B) and § 33-1121 as ceiling or spouse-administration rules, not independent asset exemptions.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not attach § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 to an asset merely because the debtors are married or the asset qualifies under another substantive exemption.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the facts show a debtor interest in an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: After classifying specific exemptions, make a separate asset-by-asset wildcard pass. Add 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for every debtor-owned asset because it covers any property, including residences, vehicles, household goods, jewelry, firearms, tools and health aids; retain every independently applicable specific federal or state citation. Its ceiling limits protected value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Skip § 522(d)(5) only when federal exemptions are unavailable or the facts do not show a debtor interest. Do not skip it because another exemption applies or the asset exceeds the ceiling.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and the debtor or debtors own an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: For every owned asset, add a separate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) output entry after evaluating specific exemptions. Evaluate that asset-exemption pair independently, so a simultaneously listed § 522(d)(1) entry does not consume the wildcard base. Use a $15,425 whole-asset ceiling for one debtor or $30,850 for two equal joint debtors, and report the lesser of the asset's value and that ceiling. Before submitting, verify that every owned asset has its (d)(5) entry alongside all specific alternatives.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 522(d)(5) when federal exemptions are unavailable, omit it because a specific exemption applies, default to $1,475 despite unused § 522(d)(1) capacity, or return only one debtor's half-interest.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: After classifying specific exemptions, make a separate § 12-1001(b) pass over every qualifying personal-property asset. Add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) alongside any motor-vehicle, necessary-apparel or prescribed-health-aid citation, as well as for jewelry and other personal property. Its $4,000 ceiling limits protected equity, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property or property the facts explicitly identify as business-use. Do not omit it because a specific exemption applies, and do not classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: After all specific subsections, make a separate § 12-1001(b) pass over every such asset. The phrase “any other property” supplies an independent alternative even when apparel, motor-vehicle, or prescribed-health-aid protection also applies. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for two equal joint debtors.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real or explicitly business-use property, omit it because another subsection applies, or replace a specific exemption with it.

by_task.when: Producing the final EC mapping after evaluating the allowable statutes for all listed assets.
by_task.procedure: For each asset separately, take the union of all independently eligible citation alternatives and emit each citation once. Return an empty array only after every applicable specific and general-property alternative has been checked.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not repeat a citation within an asset's array, copy one asset's category citations into another asset, or replace a specific exemption with a general alternative.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property.
by_task.procedure: After checking category-specific Oregon exemptions, make a separate pass over every personal-property asset and add Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p). Retain it alongside clothing, household-goods, vehicle, animal, firearm, jewelry, instrument, health-aid and other specific alternatives. Its $400 ceiling limits protected value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property. Do not omit it because another Oregon exemption applies or because the personal property's value exceeds $400.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the debtor owns a personal-property asset.
by_task.procedure: For every personal-property asset, emit a separate Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) entry in addition to every category-specific entry. Set its final whole-asset amount to the lesser of the asset's value and $400; compare the value before copying the ceiling. Verify this entry separately for each personal-property asset before submitting.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property, omit it because a specific exemption applies, output $400 when the asset is worth less, double it for joint ownership, or copy its $400 ceiling into another citation's amount.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the facts show a debtor interest in an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: After checking particular-property exemptions, make a separate § 8123 pass over every debtor-owned asset, including real property, vehicles, household goods, jewelry and business tools. Add 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 alongside every applicable specific citation; its $300 ceiling limits protected value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Skip § 8123 only when Pennsylvania exemptions are unavailable or the property is not the debtor's. Do not omit it because a specific exemption applies or the asset is worth more than $300.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the debtor or debtors own an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: For every owned asset, emit 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently and report the lesser of whole-asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for two equal joint debtors. Separately add § 8124(a)(1) only for actual wearing apparel, (a)(2) only for a Bible or school book, (a)(3) only for a qualifying sewing machine, and (a)(4) only for a service member's uniform or accoutrements.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not copy the § 8123 ceiling when the asset is worth less or omit § 8123 because another exemption applies. Do not attach any § 8124(a) paragraph to household textiles, appliances, vehicles, firearms, instruments, ordinary jewelry, or other property outside its stated class.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8124(a)(1) is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Use § 8124(a)(1) only when the asset is an actual garment or other wearing apparel.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 8124(a)(1) for household textiles, firearms, jewelry or other personal items merely because they can be worn, carried or used personally.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and facts identify a physician-authorized or professionally prescribed prosthesis, mobility device, or comparable medical aid.
by_task.procedure: Apply Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(9) and report the whole asset's value because this paragraph states no dollar ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the household-goods exemption merely because the aid is used at home, and do not apply this paragraph without facts showing the prescribed medical character.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a category-specific § 522(d) exemption is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Classify before valuing: use § 522(d)(1) for a residence up to $27,900; (d)(2) for a motor vehicle up to $4,450; (d)(3) only for household furnishings, household goods, wearing apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, up to $700 per item; (d)(4) for personal-use jewelry, up to $1,875 for one debtor or $3,750 for two equal joint debtors; (d)(6) only for actual trade tools, up to $2,800; and (d)(9) for professionally prescribed health aids at full value. Report the lesser of whole-asset value and the applicable ceiling, then retain an independent (d)(5) alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not put jewelry or firearms under (d)(3), apply (d)(6) without trade-use facts, copy a ceiling when the asset is worth less, double the (d)(2) or (d)(3) asset-level limit merely because two debtors exist, or omit the separate (d)(5) entry.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the named asset is a motor vehicle held for personal use.
by_task.procedure: Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(c) as a separate alternative and report the lesser of the whole vehicle's value and $2,400. Also retain § 12-1001(b) when its personal-property conditions are met.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 other-property ceiling for the $2,400 motor-vehicle ceiling, double the motor-vehicle amount merely because there are two debtors, or make a final allocation between separately listed vehicle candidates.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and an Oregon category-specific exemption matches the asset.
by_task.procedure: Use § 18.345(1)(a) for books, pictures, or musical instruments up to $600; (b) for wearing apparel or jewelry up to $1,800; (d) for a vehicle up to $3,000; (e) for family-use animals up to $1,000; (f) for household goods, furniture, appliances, or similar household items up to $3,000; (h) for professionally prescribed health aids at full value; § 18.362 for one firearm up to $1,000; and § 18.395(1) for an occupied homestead up to $40,000, or $50,000 when two household debtors' interests are subject. Report the lesser of whole-asset value and the applicable ceiling, and separately test § 18.345(1)(p) for personal property.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify footwear or garments as household goods, transfer the $400 general-property ceiling to a specific citation, or use the single-debtor homestead ceiling for two household debtors.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and tangible personal property is held primarily for personal, family, or household use.
by_task.procedure:
Apply Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(d) to household goods, furnishings, apparel, jewelry, adornment, appliances, books, musical instruments, firearms, sporting goods, animals, and other qualifying tangible personal property. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and the applicable $12,000 debtor ceiling; if joint ownership makes the ceiling bind, apply § 815.18(8) to each equal interest and sum the protected interests.
Execution example: When federal exemptions are also allowable, a professionally prescribed personal mobility aid can require separate entries for federal § 522(d)(9), federal § 522(d)(5), and Wisconsin § 815.18(3)(d), each valued independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit this Wisconsin alternative because a federal exemption applies, and do not use it for property the facts identify as business-use.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and the asset is a motor vehicle.
by_task.procedure: Apply Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(g) as a separate motor-vehicle alternative. Start with its $4,000 ceiling and add the unused amount of the $12,000 § 815.18(3)(d) allowance; under independent asset-exemption evaluation, no other listed asset consumes that allowance. For one debtor, report the lesser of the whole vehicle's value and $16,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not stop at $4,000 when the unused consumer-goods allowance raises the motor-vehicle ceiling, and do not add § 815.18(3)(d) to the vehicle merely because it is tangible personal property.

by_task.procedure: For every owned asset, emit 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently and report the lesser of whole-asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for two equal joint debtors. Separately add § 8124(a)(1) only for actual wearing apparel, (a)(2) only for a Bible or school book, (a)(3) only for a qualifying sewing machine, and (a)(4) only for a service member's uniform or accoutrements.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not copy the § 8123 ceiling when the asset is worth less or omit § 8123 because another exemption applies. Do not attach any § 8124(a) paragraph to household textiles, appliances, vehicles, firearms, instruments, ordinary jewelry, or other property outside its stated class.

operations.rationale: The parent omitted § 8123 from a current owned appliance solely because its value exceeded $300. The revised order separates citation eligibility from the monetary ceiling.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is a firearm, motor vehicle, apparel item, or item of jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Classify physical character before considering value: use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(10) for firearms, (8) for each motor-vehicle candidate, (1) only for actual garments or footwear, and (4) only when facts expressly identify an engagement or wedding ring. Pendants, necklaces, bracelets, earrings, lockets, brooches, and other adornments get neither (1), (4), nor household-goods § 33-1123 merely because they are worn or personal. A ceiling limits protection, not EC citation eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an otherwise matching firearm or vehicle solely for exceeding its ceiling. Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, or other non-apparel adornment as wearing apparel, and do not extend the ring exemption to jewelry that is not an engagement or wedding ring.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is a firearm, motor vehicle, apparel item, or item of jewelry.
by_task.procedure: Classify before valuing: use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(10) for firearms up to $2,000, § 33-1125(8) for each separately listed motor-vehicle candidate up to $15,000, § 33-1125(1) for actual wearing apparel up to $500, and § 33-1125(4) only for engagement or wedding rings up to $2,000. For each eligible alternative, report the lesser of the whole asset's value and its stated ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat a pendant, bracelet, watch, or other adornment as wearing apparel, extend the ring exemption to jewelry that is not an engagement or wedding ring, or perform a final allocation between separately listed vehicle candidates.

operations.rationale: The current parent again classified earrings as apparel, while earlier sources show the same confusion for other adornments and non-engagement rings. The narrower physical-character test also addresses the rejected proposal's false household-goods fallback without broadening medical or musical-instrument branches.

After checking particular-property exemptions, make a separate § 8123 pass over every debtor-owned asset, including real property, vehicles, household goods, jewelry and business tools.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is a residence, homestead-sale proceeds, or property owned by married debtors.
by_task.procedure: For a qualifying occupied homestead, use Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1101(A); for qualifying identifiable sale proceeds, separately test § 33-1101(C). Treat § 33-1101(B) and § 33-1121 as ceiling or spouse-administration rules, not independent asset exemptions.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not attach § 33-1101(B) or § 33-1121 to an asset merely because the debtors are married or the asset qualifies under another substantive exemption.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the facts show a debtor interest in an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: Initialize every debtor-owned asset's EC array with 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) before testing specific exemptions. Then add every matching specific federal or state citation; never remove (d)(5) because another citation applies or because the asset exceeds its ceiling. The ceiling limits protected value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Skip § 522(d)(5) only when federal exemptions are unavailable or the facts do not show a debtor interest. Do not skip it because another exemption applies or the asset exceeds the ceiling.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and the debtor or debtors own an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: For every owned asset, add a separate 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) output entry after evaluating specific exemptions. Evaluate that asset-exemption pair independently, so a simultaneously listed § 522(d)(1) entry does not consume the wildcard base. Use a $15,425 whole-asset ceiling for one debtor or $30,850 for two equal joint debtors, and report the lesser of the asset's value and that ceiling. Before submitting, verify that every owned asset has its (d)(5) entry alongside all specific alternatives.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 522(d)(5) when federal exemptions are unavailable, omit it because a specific exemption applies, default to $1,475 despite unused § 522(d)(1) capacity, or return only one debtor's half-interest.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: First add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) to every qualifying asset, before classifying its type or value. Retain it while adding any matching motor-vehicle, necessary-apparel, or prescribed-health-aid citation. Its $4,000 ceiling limits protected equity, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real property or property the facts explicitly identify as business-use. Do not omit it because a specific exemption applies, and do not classify jewelry as necessary wearing apparel. A personal appliance is not a trade tool without business-use facts.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: After all specific subsections, make a separate § 12-1001(b) pass over every such asset. The phrase “any other property” supplies an independent alternative even when apparel, motor-vehicle, or prescribed-health-aid protection also applies. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for two equal joint debtors.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 12-1001(b) to real or explicitly business-use property, omit it because another subsection applies, or replace a specific exemption with it.

by_task.when: Producing the final EC mapping after evaluating the allowable statutes for all listed assets.
by_task.procedure: For each asset separately, take the union of all independently eligible citation alternatives and emit each citation once. Return an empty array only after every applicable specific and general-property alternative has been checked.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not repeat a citation within an asset's array, copy one asset's category citations into another asset, or replace a specific exemption with a general alternative.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is debtor-owned personal property.
by_task.procedure: Initialize every such asset's EC array with Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) before classifying its category or considering value. Then add every matching category-specific Oregon citation; never remove (1)(p) because another exemption applies or the asset exceeds $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property. Do not omit it because another Oregon exemption applies or because the personal property's value exceeds $400.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the debtor owns a personal-property asset.
by_task.procedure: For every personal-property asset, emit a separate Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) entry in addition to every category-specific entry. Set its final whole-asset amount to the lesser of the asset's value and $400; compare the value before copying the ceiling. Verify this entry separately for each personal-property asset before submitting.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply § 18.345(1)(p) to real property, omit it because a specific exemption applies, output $400 when the asset is worth less, double it for joint ownership, or copy its $400 ceiling into another citation's amount.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the facts show a debtor interest in an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: Initialize every debtor-owned asset's EC array with 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 before checking its type or value. Then add every applicable specific citation; never remove § 8123 because another exemption applies or the asset exceeds $300. The ceiling limits protected value, not EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Skip § 8123 only when Pennsylvania exemptions are unavailable or the property is not the debtor's. Do not omit it because a specific exemption applies or the asset is worth more than $300.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the debtor or debtors own an estate asset.
by_task.procedure: For every owned asset, emit 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 independently and report the lesser of whole-asset value and $300 for one debtor or $600 for two equal joint debtors. Separately add § 8124(a)(1) only for actual wearing apparel, (a)(2) only for a Bible or school book, (a)(3) only for a qualifying sewing machine, and (a)(4) only for a service member's uniform or accoutrements.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8124(a)(1) is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Use § 8124(a)(1) only when the asset is an actual garment or other wearing apparel.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use § 8124(a)(1) for household textiles, firearms, jewelry or other personal items merely because they can be worn, carried or used personally.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and facts identify a physician-authorized or professionally prescribed prosthesis, mobility device, or comparable medical aid.
by_task.procedure: Apply Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(9) and report the whole asset's value because this paragraph states no dollar ceiling.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the household-goods exemption merely because the aid is used at home, and do not apply this paragraph without facts showing the prescribed medical character.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a category-specific § 522(d) exemption is being considered for an asset.
by_task.procedure: Classify before valuing: use § 522(d)(1) for a residence up to $27,900; (d)(2) for a motor vehicle up to $4,450; (d)(3) only for household furnishings, household goods, wearing apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, up to $700 per item; (d)(4) for personal-use jewelry, up to $1,875 for one debtor or $3,750 for two equal joint debtors; (d)(6) only for actual trade tools, up to $2,800; and (d)(9) for professionally prescribed health aids at full value. Report the lesser of whole-asset value and the applicable ceiling, then retain an independent (d)(5) alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not put jewelry or firearms under (d)(3), apply (d)(6) without trade-use facts, copy a ceiling when the asset is worth less, double the (d)(2) or (d)(3) asset-level limit merely because two debtors exist, or omit the separate (d)(5) entry.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the named asset is a motor vehicle held for personal use.
by_task.procedure: Include 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(c) as a separate alternative and report the lesser of the whole vehicle's value and $2,400. Also retain § 12-1001(b) when its personal-property conditions are met.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 other-property ceiling for the $2,400 motor-vehicle ceiling, double the motor-vehicle amount merely because there are two debtors, or make a final allocation between separately listed vehicle candidates.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and an Oregon category-specific exemption matches the asset.
by_task.procedure: Use § 18.345(1)(a) for books, pictures, or musical instruments up to $600; (b) for wearing apparel or jewelry up to $1,800; (d) for a vehicle up to $3,000; (e) for family-use animals up to $1,000; (f) for household goods, furniture, appliances, or similar household items up to $3,000; (h) for professionally prescribed health aids at full value; § 18.362 for one firearm up to $1,000; and § 18.395(1) for an occupied homestead up to $40,000, or $50,000 when two household debtors' interests are subject. Report the lesser of whole-asset value and the applicable ceiling, and separately test § 18.345(1)(p) for personal property.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify footwear or garments as household goods, transfer the $400 general-property ceiling to a specific citation, or use the single-debtor homestead ceiling for two household debtors.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and tangible personal property is held primarily for personal, family, or household use.
by_task.procedure:
Apply Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(d) to household goods, furnishings, apparel, jewelry, adornment, appliances, books, musical instruments, firearms, sporting goods, animals, and other qualifying tangible personal property. Report the lesser of the whole asset's value and the applicable $12,000 debtor ceiling; if joint ownership makes the ceiling bind, apply § 815.18(8) to each equal interest and sum the protected interests.
Execution example: When federal exemptions are also allowable, a professionally prescribed personal mobility aid can require separate entries for federal § 522(d)(9), federal § 522(d)(5), and Wisconsin § 815.18(3)(d), each valued independently.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit this Wisconsin alternative because a federal exemption applies, and do not use it for property the facts identify as business-use.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and the asset is a motor vehicle.
by_task.procedure: Apply Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(g) as a separate motor-vehicle alternative. Start with its $4,000 ceiling and add the unused amount of the $12,000 § 815.18(3)(d) allowance; under independent asset-exemption evaluation, no other listed asset consumes that allowance. For one debtor, report the lesser of the whole vehicle's value and $16,000.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not stop at $4,000 when the unused consumer-goods allowance raises the motor-vehicle ceiling, and do not add § 815.18(3)(d) to the vehicle merely because it is tangible personal property.
